newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU warns over BA/American alliance.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU warns over BA/American alliance.

text.p: The European Commission has warned Britain against approving the planned alliance between British Airways Plc and American Airlines as it stands, saying it would restrict competition.
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, in a letter to the Department of Trade and Industry, said he disagreed with Britain's announced intention to clear the deal.
He warned in his letter sent on Friday that the Commmission would defend its view in the European Court of Justice if necessary.
"At this stage of the procedure we are not convinced that the BA/AA agreement fulfills the conditions for the granting of an exemption (from EU competition rules)," the letter says.
"The conclusion of the agreement would constitute an abuse of a dominant position," it added. The proposed deal also faces strong opposition from other airlines flying lucrative transatlantic routes.

Van Miert's letter was reacting on a draft decision by Britain's Office of Fair Trading in December to allow the deal to go ahead provided the companies gave up 168 weekly takeofff and landing slots at London's Heathrow airport. BA has said it is willing to do this provided it gets financial compensation.

But in the letter to British Trade Secretary Ian Lang, Van Miert said clearly that the selling of slots was not allowed under an EU civil aviation regulations. This opinion is shared by EU Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock, EU sources said.
Nor was it enough to give up only 168 slots, one source said. He put the figure required at between 300 and 400 slots.

In past airline alliances vetted by the EU's competition watchdog, such as the takeover of Belgium's Sabena by Swissair, the Commission demanded that slot rights be made available free to rival companies.

The EU's competence to deal with the BA/American alliance has been challenged by both companies and to some extent the British authorities on the grounds that it only affects one EU state -- Britain -- and that national governments maintain jurisdiction over international civil aviation accords.
The alliance itself is conditional on an "open skies" agreement to open up air routes between Britain and the United States.
But Van Miert's letter left no doubt that if Britain formally approved the December decision, the Commission could start proceedings which could eventually end up in the European Court of Justice.

Although it would like to have sole jurisdiction in the case, the Commission cannot prevent the British authorities from carrying out their own assessment under article 85 of the EU treaty, which bans anti-competitive practices.
However, Van Miert said it would not tolerate a British decision which "conflicts" with his own preliminary analysis.

The Commission has already detailed its concerns about the deal to the companies in a statement of objections. The airlines had until Monday to comment on those objections, after which a hearing of all interested parties could be organised next month, the letter said.
A final EU ruling is not expected before the end of March, the EU sources said.
